ProofWiki explicitly states the general definition: for each point x of topological X there is some neighborhood U_x on which the entire sequence of maps to a metric M converges uniformly. The neighborhood may depend on x, and the uniform N_ε may depend on the chosen U_x as well as ε, but is NOT allowed to vary with individual points y∈U_x. Global uniform convergence implies locally uniform; converse fails on noncompact spaces generally (e.g. f_n(x)=x/n on R converges uniformly on each bounded neighborhood, not uniformly on all R). Local uniformity is stronger than mere pointwise convergence. Source also gives complex-open-disc specialization and locally uniform series via partial sums; those are contexts with additional complex-function or series prerequisites not promoted here. No local compactness, Hausdorff property, or completeness assumed by the general version, except that metric targets are Hausdorff. Empty X satisfies the condition vacuously. This independently scoped mathematical meaning is distinct from broader or stronger convergence/eigenstructure interpretations.
